title: What on Earth Is Going On?
text:
This article was featured in the One Story to Read Today newsletter. Sign up for it here. 

 “W hat on earth is going on? ” people have been asking me. First Microsoft Outlook went down ; then U.S. air traffic ; then major national banks such as Chase, Bank of America, and Wells Fargo; then United Airlines computers ; then Apple services ; and even a National Security Agency communication network . “Surely something big is going on,” people have been telling me. Is it the AI apocalypse? The first signs of a cybersecurity collapse? An attack from a rogue state? “You can’t tell me these are just coincidences,” they’re saying. That’s true; I can’t. But only because I cannot tell you much of anything about the matter.

 In the absence of actual knowledge, people (by which I mean some people, by which I mostly mean very online people) replace certain answers with desirable ones. Desirable , in this case, often means undesirable : A terrible thing that you fear or abhor becomes delightful when it affirms that your fright or abhorrence was justified. AI, for example. It threatens to disrupt, hack, take over, or replace the operations of many different systems. A belief that AI will make things worse would be affirmed by AI actually making things worse.

 The FAA definitely grounded all flights; the government says a piece of networking equipment was to blame. Perhaps you don’t believe that and think North Korea or AI or the Trump administration (or the Biden administration) is at fault instead, or in addition. All plausible explanations. Outlook definitely went down too; Microsoft issued an explanation that is too complicated to explain in detail but can be summarized as a cascading networking problem. Two “networking” problems? In one week? Seems suspicious. As the chestnut goes, if you see two ants in your kitchen, you definitely have more than two ants in your kitchen.

 Secretary of State Marco Rubio said he wouldn’t speculate on the role of artificial intelligence in the disruptions. “Every indicator we have is that every single one of these events has an explanation or a cause that has nothing to do with a cybercriminal, has nothing to do with a hostile actor or another country,” he told reporters.

 [ Juliette Kayyem: Of course Americans blamed the ground stop on AI ] 

 The proximity of these events makes them feel related. And maybe they are, in a way. Nicole Perlroth , a former cybersecurity reporter for The New York Times , suggested on CNN and X and probably elsewhere that companies are updating computer networks too quickly, after AI detects vulnerabilities. Patching them breaks something else. In the strictest sense, this explanation could make AI the hero rather than the villain, but any role that artificial intelligence might play in these matters also allows one to blame AI for causing them. Perlroth called the incidents “outages,” which is the name lots of people are using to describe the perceived pattern. Microsoft went out, the FAA went out—outages are everywhere.

 But what does an “outage” amount to? The United Airlines issue appears to have led to a minor disruption, but it had the bad fortune of occurring amid other supposedly more outage-y outages. In the case of the banks, early reports suggested that access to online accounts to review balances or schedule transfers was disrupted. Transactions carried out on card-clearing networks seemed to continue working, meaning that you could still buy blueberries at Costco. The disruption seems to have lasted less than a day, and perhaps only a few hours. Does it count as an “outage” to not be able to see your bank balance on your phone for an afternoon? Even if so, is the consequence of such an outage serious?

 This morning, the Brookings Institution’s Darrell M. West told NPR that “the whole premise” of technology companies’ business is the “trust and confidence” the public has in their systems. But this has never been true. Computer systems of all kinds have always gone down briefly. It happens every day. Why, suddenly, are people pretending that they expect every one of these machines to always work properly?

 Seeking, finding, decoding, and interpreting information that would answer these questions proves difficult. The companies have issued statements on their own and to the press, but those statements do not fully explain matters, and they feel ultimately unsatisfying or unconvincing, especially if you had come to expect or believe in a more dramatic, global calamity underlying them. Paranoiac thinking kicks in because corporate and governmental actors might be deemed fundamentally untrustworthy and duplicitous. Surely new information, always just beyond the horizon, will affirm whatever conspiracy you had in mind—or even a different one you might be delighted, which is just to say horrified, to learn about. The New York Times called the situation a “national meltdown,” a metaphor I consider overwrought but you may find understated. The paper reported that “no evidence has emerged to tie the outages together,” a statement that also affirms that nothing proves they are unconnected, either. The more you learn, the less you know.

 And atop this problem lives another: The ignorance I am earnestly expressing about the nature of these events might later be proved foolhardy if a more widespread underlying circumstance reveals itself to be responsible, or even contributory. I cannot make any definitive statements regarding “what we know” about any of what has transpired, because I know essentially nothing. It would be both irresponsible to claim that I hold greater knowledge than the none that I actually possess, and embarrassing, besides, to be proved wrong. And so the door to a Widespread Problem must remain open to the unknowable future, where discourse about it can continue.

 What asking What on earth is happening? even means is also subject to epistemological complication. If your organization uses Microsoft 365, you definitely noticed that email and calendars weren’t working. But if you weren’t trying to log in to your bank or access the full-resolution version of your iCloud photos at exactly the wrong time, you would have neither noticed a problem nor called it an “outage.” If you spend a lot of time on social media, you might have started seeing panicked posts about these issues, however, advancing the conspiratorial worry and also accelerating its dissemination. Once you know there is a problem—or think you do—a phenomenon known as the frequency illusion (sometimes called the Baader-Meinhof phenomenon) can make you think that the problem (if it is one!) is bigger than it appears. Frequency illusion combines selective attention (a mental tendency to see interesting information as high priority) and confirmation bias (the inclination to see further sightings of something as proof that it is everywhere), making your mind perceive an occasional pattern as widespread. Unless, of course, it really is everywhere , which is harder to disprove than to prove.

 While pondering the matter, I opened Facebook for reasons I cannot explain or justify. A sequence of Reels appeared, several related to the weather. One of them teased threatening, tornado-capable storms in my area, a matter I am sensitive about because of having been hit by a tornado last year. I clicked into it and a Weather Channel video came up reporting that the risk of tornadoes was a whole state away, in eastern Iowa, with storms “expected to develop Friday afternoon.” In a separate tab, I looked up the weather in Dubuque and Cedar Rapids; forecasts were for partly cloudy skies and balmy mid-autumn highs in the 60s on Friday. What was going on? I studied the video again, finally seeing that an inset freeway camera had a time stamp dated April 17. I was seeing a weather report that was seven months old, but I had to carry out investigative work even to figure out that that was the case.

 [ Read: How long until the internet breaks? ] 

 Doesn’t everyone know that Reels are engagement bait, meant to make you click and watch rather than learn and then know something? Many are entirely fake, sometimes generated by AI. In other cases, they are summoned by the algorithm, which possibly knew that I’d posted about tornadoes in the past and that I live in the Midwest. C’mon, Bogost, get a grip. This is basic 21st-century media literacy. But regardless of whether you know this, when you are inside the online-media apparatus—meant to soak up attention without regard for whether that information is inaccurate, incomplete, or downright fake—the good feeling of clarity can prove difficult to set aside.

 I closed my browser tabs and stared into the empty space of my computer desktop. What did I know, for certain, about any of this? Profoundly little. The conditions for knowledge have changed so much that knowledge itself is the thing that is melting down.

 Communication and information networks once held knowledge more closely. A major local event might be reported the next day, once, in a newspaper or on a television news show. Only the biggest would rise to national prominence. Events that burned out quickly never became newsworthy and so failed to qualify as information about which one would have knowledge. But of course the internet ended all that by allowing anyone to broadcast anything to the world, and then making every broadcast appear similarly credible.

 Anything that is feasible, cogent, or convincing enough becomes immediately elevated to the rank previously held by truth. Even proving one fact or disproving another merely feeds more suppositions into the positive feedback loop of information exchange, extending the outbreak of plausibility. Knowledge that is not yet known and that might arrive later no longer counts as clarification or affirmation, but as yet another informational option to embrace (or reject). Perhaps we will soon “learn” that hasty software patches to AI-identified vulnerabilities cascaded across the world this week. But even if we do, such knowledge will pose new opportunities for ever more fecund fields of plausible, subsequent explanation.

 Amid this glut, the lowest and most useless position to take is the one I am embracing here: that of nescience, or not knowing—and embracing the ignorance as righteous instead of treacherous or stupid. Anything is plausible, everything is possible, and therefore nothing appears to be unknowable or unknown. The loss of ignorance is tragic. Unlike computers, we may not be able to reboot it.
